items.title: Ledger Sovereignty: Debt, Accounting, and the Structure of Money in Colonial Mexican Haciendas

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article introduces the concept of “ledger sovereignty” to examine how colonial Mexican haciendas functioned as nonstate monetary institutions in contexts of chronic coin scarcity. Ledger sovereignty describes the capacity of nonstate institutions to (1) define a unit of account, (2) issue and redeem credit, (3) track obligations, and (4) enforce repayment through accounting rather than by taxation or currency issuance. Rather than treating monetary authority as exclusively state‐based, this study demonstrates how haciendas exercised de facto monetary power by monopolizing the means of specification and redemption within their own internal economies. Hacienda ledgers were not merely passive records documenting monetary transactions but actually constituted money itself, transforming subsistence and labor into a durable, debt‐based economy that bound workers to the estate. Examining the organization of credit and labor within the hacienda reveals bookkeeping itself as a technology of governance, collapsing economic calculation and social control into a single administrative framework. By highlighting the role of accounting in the creation of money, this article expands anthropological approaches to money, power, and debt beyond the state, offering a comparative framework for analyzing nonstate monetary regimes.

items.title: Christenson, Allen J., “These Are Our Roots”: The History of the K'iche’ People as Told by Lords of the Tamub' and Ilokab'
Structural Problems are Solvable Problems: Working Together to Prevent Health Inequities With a Structural Vulnerability Approach
items.affiliation: University of West Florida; Loyola University Chicago; University of Nevada, Las Vegas; University of Arizona

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Anthropologists have long grappled with how to analyze the structural production of harm. Foundational formulations of structural violence demonstrated how social forces became embodied as disparities in health and survival but were difficult to operationalize across anthropological subdisciplines. We argue that the related framework of structural vulnerability provides a tractable approach for contemporary anthropological and interdisciplinary inquiry. A structural vulnerability framework centers people, their positionalities, and experiences to better analyze who is put in harm's way. Like structural violence, structural vulnerability reframes health as a social condition rather than an individual outcome and shifts explanations of suffering toward upstream social factors that pattern risk. Unlike structural violence, structural vulnerability foregrounds existing interventions that prevent harm and promote resilience while making other possible interventions visible. Here we trace the emergence of the structural vulnerability framework, provide three concrete goals arising from it, and use biological, medical, archaeological, cultural, and forensic examples to show how it has been successfully operationalized across subdisciplines. In doing so, we show how structural vulnerability functions as a multiscalar framework that reanimates anthropological holism while supporting policy engagement. items.title: The Digital Dynamics of Language Vitality: Exploring Child‐Algorithm Interactions on YouTube and Language Shift in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan
items.affiliation: University of Michigan; University of California, Berkeley

extra.summary: ABSTRACT What is the role of children's interactions with YouTube's recommendation algorithm in language socialization, and could these interactions influence children's linguistic practices in such a way as to cause language shift? Our paper takes a mixed methodological approach to explore interactions between Kyrgyz families and YouTube, examining the reciprocal relationships between online content recommendations, offline linguistic behavior, and on/offline discourses. First, using ethnographic data, we investigate the belief that YouTube is causing language shift and the effect of this discourse on children's linguistic practices and language ideologies. Then we analyze results from an algorithmic audit of YouTube, demonstrating the proportion of Russian content presented to children. We argue that pressures from children's sociolinguistic environments cause them to prefer Russian, but children's preference for Russian is reinforced by material provided to them through YouTube's algorithm. Interactions with algorithms are language socializing and must be taken into account in situations of language shift.

items.title: Threads of Evidence: The 1928 Hurricane Victims and Ways of Knowing Them
items.affiliation: Florida Atlantic University; University of Michigan; Arizona State University; University of Miami

extra.summary: ABSTRACT In this article, the authors consider how two poorly preserved sets of skeletal remains can help us reflect on our molecular methods in bioarchaeology. These two skeletons are labeled as having come from the 1928 hurricane that hit Lake Okeechobee in Palm Beach County, Florida, drowning 2000–3000 people overnight in floodwaters from the lake. Most were Black migrant laborers. With poor skeletal preservation and no archival records for the finding of these remains, the molecular data become our best way of understanding who these individuals were. However, as the authors illustrate, molecular data can only add to the story and can only work within our own preconceived notions of identity.

items.title: States of Ambivalence: Feminist Activism, Law, and Social Media in Post‐revolution Tunisia

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Since its inception in the 1990s, the global movement against gender violence has had an uneasy relationship with power. Scholarship on the topic has emphasized the movement's involvement in dubious alliances with nonliberatory agendas, such as the carceral state or military interventions, on the one hand, or, on the other hand, its pursuit of autonomy through self‐organization. Anti–gender violence organizing in postdictatorship Tunisia tells a somewhat different story. Neither fully aligning with nor completely eschewing the state, feminists operated primarily through ambivalence. In this article, I examine the trajectory, tactics, and effects of feminist activists during the transition to democracy as they both resisted and collaborated with the state. Drawing on 18 months of ethnographic fieldwork in Tunisia and a digital ethnography, I examine feminist political action in two contrasting sites—the courts and social media—to theorize the notion of ambivalent interpellations . I argue that anti–gender violence activism in Tunisia exemplifies a particular configuration of state‐citizen relationship that is not adequately captured by the binary of domination/resistance. An ethnographic attunement to ambivalence as a political orientation brings into sharp view the duality of the state: the state as violence and the state as protection .
topics: Arab Spring and North African Politics

items.title: “What Makes It Alright to Dig Up Our Ancestral Remains?”: An Interview With Carmen Lucas, Kwaaymii Laguna Band of Indians

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Carmen Lucas is a tribal monitor, expert, and elder of the Kwaaymii Laguna Band of Indians, San Diego County, California. She learned about cultural landscapes and Ancestral human remains from her father, the late Tom Lucas—the last full‐blooded descendant of the Kwaaymii—and has been a caretaker of the Kwaaymii Homeland and burial grounds at the former Laguna Indian Reservation for the last 50 years. After a 20 year career in the United States Marine Corps, Lucas has worked in the field of cultural resource management (CRM) as a tribal monitor, consultant, and educator. She has helped archaeologists and tribal monitors to identify archaeological deposits, Ancestral remains, and burial items to promote avoidance and preservation in place. Lucas also serves on the State of California's Truth & Healing Council as a voting member. Along with historians, archaeologists, and her attorney Courtney Ann Coyle, Lucas has helped to write and successfully nominate at least five historic properties to the National Register of Historic Places based on their tribal cultural values. In this interview, Lucas provides critical insights on the role of anthropology and archaeology in CRM, especially as it relates to the development of renewable energy and mineral extraction.

items.title: Ground wars: Vegetality and the undoing of the plantation form

extra.summary: Abstract Above the banana plantations of northern Martinique, drones and satellites read the surface of the land for the stress it endures and the yield it promises. Beneath them, in soil that a synthetic pesticide has saturated for centuries to come, the ground is quietly undoing what was done to it. This lecture gives that undoing two names. The first is terrestrial knowledge , or what the ground knows: the biological intelligence that plants, insects, and microbes produce as they adapt, at temporal scales no algorithm can apprehend. The second is vegetality , or how the ground knows, and how it lives, endures, and keeps time. Drawing on more than a decade of fieldwork in Martinique, where the pesticide chlordécone lingers in the soil, the lecture follows the responses of organisms inhabiting toxic ground and argues that the plantation and the digital platform are genealogically continuous: inheritors of a single extractive grammar, both blind to what the ground does in response.

items.title: Educational abandonment under US capitalism: grassroots study of race and class in rural Metro Detroit

extra.summary: This article examines the question of race and class through an analysis of organized abandonment and more specifically, educational abandonment. Drawing from critical ethnic studies, Black geographies and Black protest thought in education, the abandonment of public education reveals how racialized geographies, rural and urban, become vulnerable to the violence of capital accumulation and sites of underdevelopment. Building from autoethnographic and archival research, the author turns to the organizing of a rural Black working-class community in Metropolitan Detroit, who during the post-Civil Rights era responded to the oppression of regional organized abandonment. Their grassroots approaches offer critical insights into how we understand history, political economy and social transformation. The author contends that under the conditions of the intensification of abandonment throughout society, it has become ever more necessary to move to a purpose of education that is rooted in collaborative study of ideology, power and the development vision of everyday people.

items.title: Governing hope: a political economy of recruitment and settlement in Philippine–Canada migration

extra.summary: Drawing on multi-sited ethnographic and qualitative research conducted between 2010 and 2025 with aspiring migrants, migrant workers, recruiters, settlement practitioners, and state representatives, this paper extends scholarship on migration industries by demonstrating how hope itself is mobilized as a productive force, linking migration governance to the reproduction of precarious labor across sending and receiving states. More precisely, we argue that labor recruitment, pre-departure orientation, and settlement services function, not as discrete interventions, but as structurally co-constituting and interconnected components of migration governance. Although rarely formally coordinated, they operate through shared institutional logics responsive to the interests of both state and capital. Priming migrants for the possibility of permanent residency while preparing them for labor market incorporation characterized by de-skilling, occupational downgrading, and precarious employment, these services cultivate and recalibrate migrant hope, and in so doing, reproduce labor market stratification while simultaneously obscuring the contradictions inherent in Canada's immigration system.

items.title: Anti‐Colonial Colonialism: Imperialist Identities of Russia and China in Their Quest for Post‐Subalternity

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Why do Russia and China legitimize colonial and imperial practices through anti‐colonial and anti‐Western rhetoric? This article compares how both regimes discursively justify coercive policies toward culturally proximate Others (Ukrainians, Taiwanese, Hongkongers) and culturally alien Others (Crimean Tatars, Uyghurs, Tibetans). It argues that colonialism is legitimized as a means of reaffirming supranational imperialist identities to pursue post‐subalternity reconstituting itself as an autonomous centre of a hierarchical order with own civilizational model as an alternative to dominant Western norms. Through processes of othering and blame‐shifting, Russia and China portray targeted populations as victims or proxies of Western neo‐colonial manipulation, framing their own domination as protective, defensive and emancipatory. This strategy, conceptualized as ‘anti‐colonial colonization’, allows both states to depict repression, assimilation and military aggression as morally necessary acts of decolonization. Drawing on discursive analysis of official and semi‐official sources, the article shows how identity‐driven colonialism legitimizes violence at home and abroad.

items.title: Re‐Signifying Soviet Monuments: State Self‐Description, Memory Politics and Ontological Security in Estonia

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Since the restoration of independence, Soviet‐era monuments in Estonia have remained contested sites through which historical legitimacy, political belonging and national identity are publicly negotiated. Following Russia's full‐scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, these monuments acquired renewed salience as Estonia moved to regulate symbols that had become flashpoints in struggles over memory and the symbolic order of the nation‐state. This article examines how Soviet monuments in Estonia are re‐signified. Drawing on a data‐driven typology‐building approach and an analytical reconstruction of salient interventions since 1991, it develops a fourfold typology of re‐signification strategies and identifies the conditions under which they de‐escalate contestation, intensify it or displace it onto other symbolic sites and issues. The article shows how semiotic mechanisms of state self‐description shape these processes and argues that monument re‐signification is central to the symbolic reproduction of political community under conditions of ontological insecurity.

items.title: Modernisation, Migration and National Identification: Evidence From Central Asia

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Under which conditions do individuals identify as citizens of a state? This paper addresses this question in the context of four Central Asia states (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan) using seven waves of Central Asia Barometer Survey Data. Despite concerns that particularistic attachments undermine nation‐building in the region, a clear majority of respondents in each country identify as citizens. Employing multilevel statistical models, the analysis tests hypotheses derived from modernisation theory and exchange‐theoretic approaches and also examines the role of group‐level structural factors. The results provide general support for modernisation‐based expectations, while also revealing a distinctive regional pattern in which rural residents are more likely than urban residents to identify as citizens. Most importantly, the findings demonstrate that transnational labour migration weakens national identification: reliance on remittances is consistently associated with a lower probability of identifying as a citizen. This result highlights a structural tension facing remittance‐dependent states, in which economic reliance on external labour markets may weaken national attachment.

items.title: Heritage languages and education in the post-migrant and post-multilingual society: Reflections from the lens of epistemic justice
items.affiliation: Eurac Research; Institute for Applied Linguistics

extra.summary: In European post-migrant and post-multilingual societies, educational institutions are generally less responsive to the transformations brought about by migration experiences and increasingly complex language interweavings. Consequently, school curricula still prioritize the languages of autochthonous communities and expect students to acquire those skills and knowledge that are legitimized. Languages associated with migranticized communities, instead, are commonly misrecognized and structurally marginalized. Within this scenario, the teaching, learning and use of non-dominant heritage languages (HLs)—languages of transnational first-, second- and third-generation speakers—offer a context for considering the role of education in perpetuating or resisting imbalances of status and power. Building on scholarship from sociolinguistics, migration studies and decolonial theories, this paper contends that educational policies and practices rooted in the misrecognition of HLs constitute forms of epistemic injustice whereby knowledges associated with dominant languages are positioned as superior, while the contributions of non-dominant communities are delegitimized. This paper first explores how epistemic injustice is interwoven into societal and institutional structures in ways that reinforce epistemic hierarchies. It does so by delineating the tensions in South Tyrol, Italy, where the three official languages—German, Italian and Ladin—coexist with a growing number of migranticized H
topics: Education and experiences of immigrants and refugees

items.title: What can linguistic justice researchers and practitioners learn from more than a century of social justice debates?

extra.summary: The concept of linguistic justice is increasingly understood by researchers and practitioners as being linked to, or part of, social justice. However, social justice itself is a contested concept that has changed definition over time, and which takes numerous, sometimes incommensurable, forms today. This article thus aims to support linguistic justice researchers and practitioners to understand and clarify how they conceptualize social justice. To do this, I provide a brief cross-disciplinary overview of major debates surrounding the concept of social justice, starting from the terms’ first appearance in the nineteenth century. In doing so I explore three significant forms of social justice from the nineteenth to the twenty-first centuries: reactionary justice, global justice, and decolonial justice. I then examine the implications that these different approaches have for how we theorize and pursue linguistic justice. In doing so, this article aims to provide bibliographic, terminological, and conceptual resources for anyone wishing to develop a more robust and transparent approach to linking social justice and linguistic justice in their work.

items.title: Savage capital: Cannibal urbanization in the Peruvian Amazon

extra.summary: This paper develops the concept of cannibal urbanization to capture the distinctive urban process at work within the hidden abodes of planetary urbanization. It does so through an exploration of the relationship between extractivism and urbanization in the case of the city of Iquitos and its surrounding resource frontiers in the Peruvian Amazon. The largest city in the world unreachable by road, Iquitos is a money laundering centre for narcotrafficking; a logistical node for illegal logging and gold mining; and a spatial mechanism of systemic corruption through which the mafias that control these industries access oil rents via the construction of public works. The original wealth of this settler colonial city was based on the enslavement and extermination of the Indigenous peoples of the region during the Peruvian rubber boom, and the city and its constitutive frontiers continue to be marked by multiple forms of direct violence, in addition to the slow violence inflicted through urban ruination and ecological breakdown. Drawing on sixteen months of ethnographic research conducted between 2019 and 2023, I interpret Iquitos as embodying the urban dimension of cannibal capitalism, understood as the regime of accumulation characteristic of the hidden abodes of planetary urbanization. I argue that cannibal urbanization is based on both the anthropophagous exploitation of racialized human beings and an autophagous world ecology that progressively cannibalizes the underlying socioe

items.title: MARKAZIY OSIYONING KICHIK ETNIK GURUHLARINI O‘RGANISH MUAMMOLARI: XIX–XX ASRLARGA OID TADQIQOTLARNING TARIXSHUNOSLIK TAHLILI

extra.summary: The article presents a historiographical review of studies devoted to the small ethnic groups of Central Asia, covering the period from the second half of the nineteenth century to the late 1980s. It analyzes the gradual development of scholarly knowledge concerning the region’s ethnic minorities, including Bukharan Jews, Central Asian Arabs, Iranians, Uyghurs, Koreans, Turkmens, and others. Particular attention is paid to a critical examination of the ideological constraints imposed on Soviet ethnography, its emphasis on the “remnants” of tribal social structures, and its simplified interpretation of cultural dynamics. The article concludes that, despite their methodological limitations, the reviewed scholarly works constitute a valuable empirical foundation for reconstructing the ethnic landscape of the region under colonial rule and Soviet modernization. Furthermore, the study identifies significant gaps in research approaches resulting from insufficient attention to the internal differentiation and adaptation strategies of small ethnic groups and outlines promising directions for future research in this field.

items.title: NILAI-NILAI KEARIFAN LOKAL DALAM RITUAL MAPPADEKKO PADA MASYARAKAT ADAT KELURAHAN TORO KECAMATAN TANETE RIATTANG TIMUR: KAJIAN ETNOLINGUISTIK

extra.summary: This study examines local wisdom values represented in the Mappadekko ritual among the Indigenous community of Toro, Tanete Riattang Timur, Bone Regency, through an ethnolinguistic perspective. The study was motivated by the need to document local cultural heritage and explain how language and ritual practices convey community values amid modernization. This research employed a qualitative approach with an ethnographic design. Data were gathered through participant observation, in-depth interviews with customary figures and ritual participants, audio-visual recording, documentation, and literature review. The data were analyzed by connecting linguistic forms, ritual actions, and their socio-cultural contexts through data reduction, display, and conclusion drawing. The findings indicate that Mappadekko is organized into preparation, implementation, and closing stages. Linguistic data include culturally specific terms such as mappadekko, ase, palungeng, and Dewata Seuwae, as well as ritual utterances expressing permission, humility, gratitude, and togetherness. The local wisdom values identified include religiosity and gratitude, social solidarity and mutual cooperation, moral conduct, ecological awareness, and cultural identity. The ritual therefore functions not only as a post-harvest cultural practice but also as a medium for transmitting knowledge and values across generations. items.title: Stakeholder-Oriented Ecotourism Management and Marketing: A Sustainability Performance Evaluation of Chengyang Eight Villages in Guangxi, China

extra.summary: As ecotourism destinations face increasing market competition and growing sustainability pressures, destination managers must balance stakeholder interests while converting ecological, sociocultural, and economic resources into sustainable market value. Drawing on stakeholder theory, strategic management, and destination marketing perspectives, this study develops a stakeholder-oriented sustainability performance evaluation framework for ecotourism management. Fourteen indicators across economic, sociocultural, and environmental dimensions are constructed through a literature review and evaluated from the perspective of indigenous residents as core stakeholders. Using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Likert-scale survey data, and Chengyang Eight Villages in Guangxi, China as the empirical setting, the study assesses the relative managerial priorities of sustainable ecotourism development. The reported dimension weights assign the highest priority to economic sustainability, followed by sociocultural sustainability, whereas environmental sustainability receives the lowest relative weight. Discrepancies between the displayed matrices and indicator weights require reconciliation before the indicator rankings can be treated as definitive. The reported weighting structure highlights differences in the relative emphasis assigned to livelihood, cultural, and environmental considerations, creating important implications for destination governance, market positioning, service exp

items.title: Social capital grounded in forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation and household livelihood resilience in rural border areas: evidence from southern Xinjiang, China
items.affiliation: Zhejiang Sci-Tech University; Zhejiang University of Science and Technology; Zhejiang Normal University; Xinjiang Institute of Technology

extra.summary: How community building relates to household livelihood resilience is an important question for multiethnic border regions. We examine this question by measuring social capital grounded in forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation (FSC-CN) using 2025 survey data from 591 households in four prefectures of southern Xinjiang. We compare this contextualized measure with a conventional social-capital benchmark and examine its dimensions, resource pathways, and livelihood differences. We find a significant positive association with resilience that persists after household-resource adjustment and the exclusion of potentially overlapping content from both indices. The contextualized measure also provides additional explanatory information beyond the conventional benchmark. Dimension-level analysis identifies significant independent associations for relational and structural capital, while sequential-path estimates connect cognitive orientations with resilience through relational capital. This combination highlights how shared orientations are connected to reciprocal relationships and organizational networks. We further find positive digital-capability and policy-benefit paths, with the clearest evidence for digital capability. The stronger association among households with more rural-oriented livelihoods underscores the relevance of social connections where production information and cooperation are recurrent needs. items.title: Do guard dogs really need protecting? Tibetan perspectives and practices of Tibetan Mastiff conservation after the market collapse
items.source: Environment and Planning E Nature and Space
items.affiliation: London School of Economics and Political Science

extra.summary: Following the collapse of the Tibetan Mastiff (TM) market in China in the mid-2010s, conservation of the breed has become a laissez-faire field dominated by competing grassroots actors. Drawing on twenty-four months of multi-sited ethnography in Tibetan pastoral communities, breeding farms, and enthusiast networks, this article compares how Tibetan intellectuals, enthusiasts, and pastoralists in Machu (Gansu) understand whether TMs need conservation, who should be responsible for it, and by what method. Because the TM is neither a wildlife species nor a standardised breed, what stakeholders seek to sustain is a working pastoral lineage and the interspecies lifeway through which guarding capabilities are cultivated. I argue that these positions are best distinguished through three concepts routinely conflated in everyday speech: guarding, protection, and conservation. Tibetan intellectuals use the TM as a metaphor for Tibetan dispossession but rarely offer practical proposals. Tibetan enthusiasts, despite claiming Tibetan custodianship, equate conservation with protection through controlled breeding farms, reproducing the paternalistic rescue logic critiqued by Abu-Lughod. Pastoralist conservationists in Machu instead seek to restore the conditions in which guard dogs can guard once again, although certain pastoral dog-keeping practices such as long-term tethering and misconceptions about canine health may compromise individual dog welfare. items.title: La Región Autónoma del Tibet (RAT)y la sucesión del dalái lama en la geopolíticade la República Popular China (RPCh)

extra.summary: The text analyzes the geopolitical importance of the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), also known as the Xizang Autonomous Region in the official Chinese transcription, based on the debate surrounding the succession of the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso. In 2025, he declared that his reincarnation would take place outside of PRCh and would be under the exclusive control of his office in India. This decision intensifies the dispute with the Chinese government, which claims authority over the process through historical and legal mechanisms, highlighting a conflict that transcends the religious sphere and becomes part of the struggle for political legitimacy and sovereignty. Historically, the relationship between Tibet and China has fluctuated between autonomy and control, the latter becoming more entrenched after the territory’s incorporation into the PRCh in 1950 and the Dalai Lama’s exile in 1959. Currently, the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) holds significant strategic value due to its geographic location, natural resources, and growing industrial development, making it a key territory for PRCh’s security, economic development, and international projection. The document concludes that the Dalai Lama’s succession could lead to a situation of “dual legitimacy,” exacerbating regional tensions. items.title: Supply-Demand Preferences and Compatibility between Sending and Recipient Parties in Shanghai–Yunnan Group-Based Paired Education Assistance

extra.summary: To examine the supply-demand matching status of the Shanghai–Yunnan “group-based” paired education assistance and to identify the supply-demand misalignments and their generative mechanisms between the sending and recipient parties, this study draws on supply-demand adaptation theory to construct an analytical framework of “supply preference—demand preference—supply-demand adaptation status—causes of contradiction—optimization path.” Employing a mixed-methods design that combines a two-sided supply-demand importance matrix, independent-samples t-tests, and NVivo qualitative coding, the study uses 40 questionnaires from Shanghai teachers dispatched to Yunnan and 52 questionnaires from local teachers in recipient county-level general senior high schools in Yunnan as its primary data, triangulated with policy documents, symposium interviews, and typical assistance cases. The findings show that the two parties are highly aligned in teacher team building and curriculum resource development; significant cognitive misalignment emerges in the dimension of school management systems and institutional export, which falls into the Supply Surplus Zone; hardware facilities and teaching equipment support fall into the Supply Gap Zone; and the compatibility between policy and local learning conditions and the rationality of the assessment mechanism constitute the major practical obstacles. The supply-demand misalignment is rooted in the developmental gap in education between eastern and west

items.title: Digital Competence Development for Information Engineering Students in Higher Education Institutions in Yunnan Province: A Research Framework and Preliminary Exploration
items.affiliation: Kunming University of Science and Technology; Srinakharinwirot University

extra.summary: With the deepening of global digital transformation and the advancement of China's "Digital Yunnan" strategy, digital competence has become a core competency for information engineering students to adapt to industrial upgrading and national development needs. This study examines digital competence development in four higher education institutions in Yunnan Province through a diagnostic survey, expert consultation, and a single-group pretest-posttest intervention. The diagnostic survey retained 413 valid responses from institutions with a combined information engineering enrollment of 5,621. The framework integrates Digital Awareness, Digital Knowledge, Digital Skills, Digital Security, and Digital Ethics and connects these dimensions to international frameworks and engineering education. Following an eight-session, 24-hour program, 30 students at Kunming University of Science and Technology reported higher overall competence at posttest (M = 3.52, SD = 0.41) than at pretest (M = 3.01, SD = 0.46), t(29) = 8.716, p < .001. Digital Security and Digital Skills showed the largest reported relative gains. These findings provide preliminary evidence of change following the program. The absence of a comparison group and delayed assessment limits causal interpretation, evidence of retention, and generalization beyond the participating institutions.

items.title: Ethnic traditional sports participation, cultural identity, and psychological wellbeing among Chinese minority adolescents: a moderated mediation model

extra.summary: Ethnic traditional sports constitute a distinctive vehicle for cultural transmission and physical activity among ethnic minority youth, yet their psychological correlates remain underexplored. This study examined whether cultural identity statistically mediates the relationship between ethnic traditional sports participation and psychological wellbeing among Chinese minority adolescents, and whether this indirect pathway is moderated by perceived social support. A total of 1,086 secondary school students (522 boys, 564 girls, M age = 14.26 years, SD = 1.38) from six schools in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region completed anonymous questionnaires measuring ethnic traditional sports participation, cultural identity, perceived social support, and psychological wellbeing. Moderated mediation analysis was conducted using the PROCESS macro (Model 14) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Participation in ethnic traditional sports was positively associated with cultural identity ( β = 0.46, p < 0.001), which in turn was associated with psychological wellbeing ( β = 0.37, p < 0.001). The participation–identity link and the identity–wellbeing link combined to form a significant indirect effect [ β = 0.168, 95% bootstrap CI (0.137, 0.200)]. items.affiliation: INTI International University; Sukhothai Thammathirat Open University; Mahsa University

Qualitative research design is implemented in this study. These include analysis of policy document as well as comparative studies from China, Malaysia and Thailand (henceforth abbreviated as CMT) drawing out exemplary cases of good practices as well as comparison through cross-case analysis on the educational equity policies for underprivileged and/or ethnic minority groups in CMT that had major education reforms implemented recently especially between 2024 and 2026 in preparation for Industrial Revolution (IR). Drawing on Rawls's (1971) principle of compensatory justice also Fraser's (2008) two-dimensional framework of redistribution and recognition, the study examines how each country addresses enrollment opportunities, language, cultural adaptation, and the tension between national cohesion, cultural diversity as well as digital divide issues to access curriculum integrating emerging CT. items.title: Dynamic Linkages Among China’s “PLV” Exports
items.affiliation: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology

extra.summary: Photovoltaic products, lithium batteries, and new energy vehicles, collectively known as China’s “PLV” exports, have become important drivers of the country’s foreign trade development. Their close industrial linkages make understanding the dynamic interactions among their exports essential for examining cross-industry coordination and export competitiveness. Using monthly panel data for 30 Chinese provincial-level regions from 2017 to 2024, excluding Tibet, Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan, this paper constructs a panel vector autoregression (PVAR) model and conducts an empirical analysis using Granger causality tests, impulse response functions, and variance decomposition. The results show significant dynamic interactions among exports of the “PLV.” (1) Photovoltaic products and lithium battery exports have significant Granger-cause NEV exports, highlighting the supporting role of related industries in the development of China’s NEV exports. (2) Bidirectional Granger causality exists between photovoltaic exports and the lithium battery-new energy vehicle coupling system, and between lithium battery exports and the photovoltaic-new energy vehicle coupling system, highlighting the potential for cross-industry synergy. (3) The interactions among the three exhibit differentiated time lags. New energy vehicles and lithium batteries respond quickly, while photovoltaic exports show a lagged strengthening pattern. items.title: The Ontological Turn in Transformative Learning: Rethinking Inner Transformation Through Meister Eckhart

extra.summary: While Mezirow’s foundational model frames transformative learning as a primarily epistemic process of shifting meaning perspectives through critical reflection, subsequent critiques have highlighted the need to expand this theory. This paper explores how Meister Eckhart’s works can serve as a dialogical resource for a more ontological understanding of transformation. Drawing on a selective reading of four Eckhartian concepts, the paper interprets transformative learning as a process of relational becoming marked by non-possessiveness, release, surrender, receptivity, and openness. It challenges instrumentalist and performative tendencies that seek to control, produce or measure inner changes. By reframing inner transformation as an emergent, ontological process, this paper proposes a pedagogy of release. Engaging Eckhart in dialogue enables transformative learning theory to foreground depth, hiddenness, and unpredictability, shifting the focus from perspective change to transformation of being in relation.

items.title: Rethinking sociolinguistics beyond positivist anthropocentrism

extra.summary: The differences between van Oostendorp’s response and my article are methodological and theoretical. They concern divergent ways of analysing interspecies and intraspecies interaction. The tensions that emerge are productive and reveal the challenges involved in rethinking sociolinguistics beyond anthropocentric assumptions. Whereas the response emphasizes and proceeds from a positivist operationalisation perspective, my multispecies ethnographical article explicitly questions some of the assumptions that inform such a perspective. Because of this difference in framing, the article and the response operate in different registers: the response deploys criteria that eschew the theoretical and methodological intervention the article seeks to make. While van Oostendorp and I may disagree about which frameworks are best suited to understanding these capacities in nonhuman animals in this day and age, I argue we cannot judge one framework—a sociolinguistic ethnographic one—by using the standards of another, namely a positivist framework.

items.title: Domestication in the Making: Urban Chinese Young Adults and Companion Cats

extra.summary: Abstract Against the backdrop of cats emerging as the primary nonhuman companion animals among urban young adults in China, existing studies, largely framed by functionalism, tend to overlook feline subjectivity. Drawing on multispecies ethnography, this article mobilizes “domestication” as a conceptual placeholder and, through participant observation, in-depth interviews, and online ethnography, traces the ongoing making of domestication in youth-cat relations. The findings reveal that domestication, in practice, comprises repeated repair work encompassing care, conflict, and negotiation. In relationships, embodied exchanges such as touch and mutual gaze foster cross-species empathy and temperament cultivation, yet they also carry the risk of narcissistic projection. In place, domus-making – through spatial yielding, object re-scripting, and ritual memory – extends multispecies kinship and brings a “multispecies family” into being, even as the return of “wildness” keeps household boundaries in motion. Domestication thus unfolds within mutuality, uncertainty, and continual tinkering.

items.title: A framework for Māori knowledge in research, science and technology: revisited

extra.summary: Background: Earlier work published in 2000 developed a taxonomy for positioning Research, Science and Technology (RS&T) projects along a continuum from mainstream to kaupapa Māori.1 Aim: To revisit and extend this framework by incorporating recent developments in ontology, mātauranga Māori scholarship, and methodological approaches to knowledge engagement. Methods: This paper undertakes a conceptual analysis drawing on three key developments: the Ontological Turn in social science; the expansion of mātauranga Māori scholarship to include empirical, interpretive, critical, and transcendent domains; and the methodological shift from synthesis and interface models towards composition. Results: The Ontological Turn provides a basis for recognising that Māori inhabit a distinct world of reality, rather than offering a cultural perspective on a shared world. Mātauranga Māori scholarship further differentiates forms of knowledge, including covenantal (whakapapa-grounded) and revelational (atua and tīpuna-sourced) knowledge as legitimate epistemic authorities. The move to composition clarifies how Māori and Western knowledge systems may engage without assimilation. These developments are integrated into an expanded framework that retains the original four-category taxonomy while strengthening its epistemological and ontological foundations. items.title: Composing Assemblages and Engaging Time in Hindu Ritual: Ritual Aesthetics in Nepal
items.affiliation: Adelaide University; The University of Adelaide

extra.summary: This article is concerned with elaborating a novel theoretical account of Hindu ritual in Nepal which takes as its starting point the ethnographic and theoretical work of Vivienne Kondos. It does so by (re)contextualising her account through an array of new concepts, drawing, most notably, from the ontological turn, Handelman and Kapferer’s ritual aesthetics, Deleuze and Guattari’s pragmatics, and comparative perspectives on Hindu cosmology. Hindu cosmology conceptualises the world as an entropic flux generated through processes of creative fragmentation. To contact divinity in ritual (for whatever purpose) one must move through temporal processes of cosmic death and rebirth. This is achieved through the composition of ritual assemblages. Such assemblages engage invention (sensu Wagner) and elucidating their composition requires a conceptualisation of time, transgression, sacrifice and personhood. With these theoretical tools and ethnographic context, anthropological accounts of power and performativity in ritual can be pushed towards more generative lines of analysis.

items.title: Between Humanism and Market Naturalism: Adam Smith in Karl Polanyi’s The Great Transformation
items.source: Erasmus Journal for Philosophy and Economics

extra.summary: On the 250th anniversary of The Wealth of Nations, this article revisits Adam Smith’s legacy by examining his reception in Karl Polanyi’s The Great Transformation. While Polanyi sharply criticizes Smith for contributing to the naturalization of market exchange, he simultaneously presents Smith as a thinker whose political economy rests on humanistic foundations. The article reconstructs this apparent tension by critically examining Polanyi’s reception of Smith’s anthropology, theory of the division of labour, and conception of wealth. It argues that Polanyi offers a largely convincing account of Smith’s rejection of economic naturalism, while misreading Smith’s account of human motivation. The paper concludes that Smith is understood as a transitional figure: the founder of political economy whose thought remains subordinate to social purposes and therefore cannot alone ground the idea of a fully self-regulating market. This interpretation contributes to contemporary philosophical debates on market society and economic embeddedness.

items.title: Cosmic Sensibility for Cosmopolitics: Making Sense in the Anthropocene
items.affiliation: Lithuanian Academy of Music and Theatre

extra.summary: In response to Philippe Descola’s call for a cosmopolitics adequate to the crisis of the multiscalar Anthropocene, this paper interrogates the problem of entangled coexistence by shifting the analytical register to sensibility. The paper therefore proposes the speculative concept of cosmic sensibility, which mobilizes sense as constitutive of cosmopolitics and names a relational openness through which distinct entities become mutually sense-able without necessarily presupposing their commensurability. The concept synthesizes insights from the ontological turn (Descola, Viveiros de Castro, Hui), process-relational cosmology (Whitehead) and cosmopolitics (Stengers), as well as feminist STS (Barad, Haraway), in order to sketch its provisional contours across three interconnected registers: onto-epistemological, cosmopolitical, and ethical. Reading in parallel a line of authors who rethink the anthropocentric assumptions of the cosmos in relational terms, the paper contends that ontological plurality becomes cosmopolitically consequential only insofar as agents inhabiting heterogeneous worlds can enter into relations of mutual sense-ability. Cosmic sensibility thus reframes entangled coexistence as a practice of dwelling halfway, sustaining difference while remaining response-able to the worldings produced through the encounter.

items.title: Liminal familyhood: Conceptualizing the gray zone between marriage and divorce in late-modern societies

extra.summary: This study aims to conceptualize a relational form that has remained undefined within the sociology of family literature by focusing on the gray area situated between marriage and divorce. While existing scholarship examines transformations in family structures through the lenses of individualization, liquid relationships, and emotional capitalism, it has largely overlooked the chronic forms of uncertainty embedded between marriage and divorce. In response to this gap, the study introduces the concept of liminal familyhood to explain conditions in which marriage continues legally despite relational, emotional and everyday disengagement. Reinterpreting the classical anthropological theory of liminality from the perspective of family sociology, the study draws upon Arnold Van Gennep’s theory of rites of passage, Victor Turner’s concept of anti-structure, and Arpad Szakolczai’s notion of permanent liminality. The insecurity and uncertainty characterizing intimate relationships in late modernity are analyzed through Anthony Giddens’ concept of the pure relationship , Zygmunt Bauman’s liquid love , Eva Illouz’s emotional capitalism , and Ulrich Beck and Elisabeth Beck-Gernsheim’s theory of individualization . The study argues that liminality within contemporary family relationships has evolved from a temporary transitional phase into a structural and enduring relational condition.
